Definition of GIS
A Geographic Information System (GIS) is a computer-based system designed to capture, store, 
manage, analyze, and visualize data that is linked to a location on the Earth's surface.
It answers four fundamental geographic questions:

What is at a given location?

Where does a particular feature or condition occur?

What has changed over time at a location?

What patterns exist and what do they mean?
Evolution of GIS (Key milestones)

Pre-GIS Era (Before 1960s) — Paper Maps Geography relied entirely on hand-drawn maps. 
Overlaying, updating, or analysing spatial data was slow, manual, and error-prone. There was no 
way to store or query geographic data digitally.

1960s — Birth of GIS Roger Tomlinson developed the Canada Geographic Information System 
(CGIS) — the world's first true GIS — to analyse land capability data across Canada. This 
introduced the revolutionary idea of storing geographic data digitally and linking it to attributes. 
Tomlinson is widely called the "Father of GIS."

1970s–80s — Institutional & Desktop GIS: GIS moved from mainframe computers to 
workstations. ESRI (founded 1969) released early commercial software, making GIS accessible to 
governments, universities, and businesses.

spatial analysis.
Components of GIS

Hardware — the physical equipment GIS runs on. This includes computers that process and store 
data, GPS devices that capture location in the field, scanners that digitize paper maps, and servers 
that host GIS databases. Essentially, anything you can touch.

Software — the programs that make GIS work. Examples include ArcGIS (industry standard, 
commercial), QGIS (free and open-source), and Google Earth Engine (cloud-based).

ly, anything you can touch.

Software — the programs that make GIS work. Examples include ArcGIS (industry standard, 
commercial), QGIS (free and open-source), and Google Earth Engine (cloud-based). Software 
handles everything from displaying maps to running complex spatial analysis.

Data — the fuel of any GIS. It comes in two forms: spatial data (the "where" — coordinates, shapes, 
locations) and attribute data (the "what" — descriptions, values, and labels attached to those 
locations). For example, a hospital's location is spatial; its name, capacity, and type are attributes.

People — the human element. This ranges from field technicians collecting data, to GIS analysts 
building models, to managers and policymakers using the outputs to make decisions. A GIS is only 
as useful as the people who design and interpret it.

Methods — the procedures and workflows used to collect, process, and analyze data. This 
includes things like which projection system to use, how to overlay layers, or which analysis model 
fits a problem. Methods ensure results are accurate and repeatable.
Core Concepts of GIS
Spatial Thinking — this is the mental framework that underpins everything in GIS. It means reasoning 
about the world in terms of:

Location — where is something?

Distance — how far apart are things?

tial Thinking — this is the mental framework that underpins everything in GIS. It means reasoning 
about the world in terms of:

Location — where is something?

Distance — how far apart are things?


Direction — which way, relative to what?

Pattern — do features cluster, scatter, or align?

Relationship — how do features interact with or influence each other?
It's not just a GIS skill — it's a way of asking geographic questions. For example, "why are flood incidents 
concentrated in this neighbourhood?" is spatial thinking in action. GIS is simply the tool that helps answer 
those questions computationally.
Layers & Map Abstraction — GIS represents the real world by breaking it into separate, thematic layers, 
each holding one type of feature. For example:

Roads layer

Rivers layer

Land use layer

Population density layer
Each layer can be studied alone or stacked and combined with others to reveal patterns that wouldn't be 
visible in a single map.

Each layer can be studied alone or stacked and combined with others to reveal patterns that wouldn't be 
visible in a single map. This is called abstraction — simplifying a complex reality into manageable, 
organised slices of information.
A classic analogy is a stack of transparencies — each sheet shows one theme, but overlaying them 
builds a richer picture of the world.
Together, spatial thinking tells you what questions to ask, and layers give you the structure to answer them.
Applications of GIS
Agriculture GIS helps farmers and agronomists make data-driven decisions by mapping and monitoring 
the land:

Crop monitoring — tracking growth, health, and stress using satellite imagery

Soil mapping — identifying soil types and fertility across fields to guide fertiliser use

Yield prediction — analysing past and current conditions to forecast harvests

Information Technology GIS powers location-aware systems and smart digital infrastructure:

Spatial databases — storing and querying data with a geographic component

Smart applications — ride-hailing apps, delivery routing, and real-estate platforms all rely on GIS 
under the hood

Fleet tracking — monitoring vehicles in real time using GPS-linked GIS

Location APIs — services like Google Maps API that embed spatial functionality into other 
software
Environmental & Urban Planning GIS is essential for managing land, resources, and growing cities:

Flood risk mapping — identifying vulnerable areas to guide infrastructure and emergency planning

Urban growth modelling — simulating how cities expand to inform zoning decisions

Conservation — mapping habitats and biodiversity to prioritise protected areas
GIS Workflow Overview
The GIS workflow is a five-stage pipeline that takes raw information and turns it into actionable output:
1. Data Collection — gathering raw geographic information through field surveys, satellite remote sensing, 
GPS tracking, or existing datasets.
